newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Jewish decision on Swiss banks boycott in weeks.
newsitem.headline: Jewish decision on Swiss banks boycott in weeks.

text.p: A Jewish leader said on Tuesday he would decide in four weeks whether to call for a boycott against Swiss banks in response to a blackmail charge by a Swiss leader over World War Two compensation for Jews.

Jewish Agency chairman Avraham Burg blasted Swiss leaders for refusing to apologise for the blackmail remark by Economic Minister Jean-Pascal Delamuraz. He said he would not take part in a joint commission's search for dormant accounts in Swiss banks left by Jewish victims of the Nazi Holocaust.
"The Swiss are again playing with words, attacking marginal issues and ignoring the central issues," Burg said through a spokeswoman.

"They're trying to buy us with money that's not theirs," he said after the Swiss government announced it wanted to "put to a proper use" around 40 million Swiss francs ($30 million) it found in dormant bank accounts.
Swiss bank shares fell on Monday in what some traders said was a response to Jewish calls for a boycott of Swiss banks.
"As for now, the partial boycott was suggested, economic disinvestment...and things like this were suggested to us," said Burg, laying out possible responses to the blackmail remark.
"We analyse each and every one of them. We'll come with our recommendation for action within four weeks," he told reporters after meeting in Jerusalem the Swiss ambassador to Israel.
Swiss banking officials and Jewish leaders agreed last May to hunt together for money Jews deposited in Swiss accounts before being killed in Nazi concentration camps during World War Two.
The joint Swiss-Jewish commission, headed by former U.S. Federal Reserves chairman Paul Volcker, includes Burg, other Jewish leaders and Swiss bankers.
Delamuraz described Jewish demands for a $250 million bank fund to compensate families of Holocaust victims as "extortion and blackmail."
"Such a fund would be considered an admission of guilt," he said just before ending a one-year rotating term as his country's president last month.
Delamuraz said Jewish American officials had proposed the fund to special ambassador Thomas Border. Burg said Jewish leaders were only seeking justice.

"We are going to settle once and forever the moral and economic commitment that we have to families, fathers, mothers who have perished in the Holocaust," Burg told reporters, saying his own grandmother was murdered by Nazis.
Six million Jews were killed in Nazi concentration camps during World War Two.
"Not even one dime or dollar or Swiss franc...which was done in an unjust way will remain in their safety vaults," he said.
Burg said he could not participate in talks with Swiss officials as long as members of the Volcker committee did not denounce Delamuraz's comments.
"It will be almost impossible for us to sit together around the same table with people who did not deny, did not regret and did not oppose the president calling me a blackmailer."
He said the silence by members of the joint commission could be construed as support for Delamuraz's remarks.
"Maybe there were some people hiding behind the back of the president, happy that the president is actually breaking the process which is going to be a very dear one to some of these people.
"If this is not the case, please, my partners, prove it," Burg added.
